records.topic: What If You Lived on the Space Station?
records.hook: Why the space station circles Earth every 93 minutes.
records.openingLine: Why the space station circles Earth every 93 minutes.
records.secondBeat: That's 15.5 orbits, and sunrises, every day.
records.scientificMechanism: the station free-falls around Earth at orbital speed, circling the planet many times a day
records.scenarioChange: someone lived aboard the ISS for months
records.expectedConsequence: about 15.5 sunrises a day, weightlessness and a tightly scheduled life
records.coreQuestion: If you lived on the space station, how many sunrises would you see each day?
records.misconception: Astronauts aren't weightless because there's no gravity; they're falling around Earth.
editorialTitles: Life Where the Sun Rises 15 Times a Day
Why the Space Station Never Stops Falling

facts.claim: Its orbit takes it at 7.67 km/s (27,600 km/h; 17,200 mph) roughly every 93 minutes around Earth, 15.5 times a day.
The station orbits between 51.64° north and south, at about 400 kilometres (250 miles) above Earth, below the Van Allen radiation belts.
The Integrated Truss Structure connects the station's solar panels and radiators to its 16 major pressurized modules.
The station is expected to remain operational until the end of 2030.

narration.text: Why the space station circles Earth every 93 minutes.
That's 15.5 orbits, and sunrises, every day.
It flies at 27,600 kilometres per hour.
It's only about 400 kilometres up.
Crews aren't beyond gravity; they're constantly falling around Earth.
Days and nights blur, so schedules replace the Sun.
The station is due to operate until the end of 2030.
So living in orbit means living in permanent free fall.

records.topic: What If a 90-Day Rover Lasted 14 Years?
records.hook: Why a 90-sol rover kept going 14 years.
records.openingLine: Why a 90-sol rover kept going 14 years.
records.secondBeat: Opportunity lasted 57 times its designed lifespan.
records.scientificMechanism: careful power management and dust-clearing winds kept a solar-powered rover running far beyond its design life
records.scenarioChange: a rover designed for 90 sols kept driving for years
records.expectedConsequence: a marathon-length journey until a planet-wide dust storm cut its power
records.coreQuestion: If a 90-day rover lasted 14 years, what finally stopped it?
records.misconception: Opportunity wasn't built to last; it outlived its plan 57 times over.
editorialTitles: The Mars Rover That Refused to Quit
How Opportunity Outlived Its Plan 57 Times

facts.claim: Opportunity is a robotic rover that was active on Mars from 2004 until 2018.
Opportunity was operational on Mars for 5111 sols (14 years, 138 days on Earth).
This careful operation allowed Opportunity to operate for 57 times its designed lifespan.
Mission highlights included the initial 90-sol mission, finding meteorites, and over two years of exploring and studying Victoria crater.

narration.text: Why a 90-sol rover kept going 14 years.
Opportunity lasted 57 times its designed lifespan.
It stayed active on Mars from 2004 all the way to 2018.
That's 5111 sols of work.
Winds sometimes cleaned dust off its solar panels.
In 2018, a planet-wide dust storm starved it of power.
So careful engineering can outlast every plan.

records.topic: What If Mars Got a Ring?
records.hook: Why Phobos circles Mars in under 8 hours.
records.openingLine: Why Phobos circles Mars in under 8 hours.
records.secondBeat: It orbits just 6,000 kilometres above the surface.
records.scientificMechanism: tidal forces slowly drag Phobos inward until they tear it apart
records.expectedConsequence: a temporary ring of debris circling Mars
records.coreQuestion: If Mars got a ring, where would it come from, and how long would it last?
records.misconception: Moons don't always drift away; Phobos is spiralling in.
editorialTitles: The Moon That's Falling Into Mars
Why Mars May Get a Ring

facts.claim: It orbits 6,000 km (3,700 mi) from the Martian surface, closer to its primary body than any other known natural satellite to a planet.
It orbits Mars much faster than Mars rotates and completes an orbit in just 7 hours and 39 minutes.
Tidal deceleration is gradually decreasing the orbital radius of Phobos by approximately 2 m (6 ft 7 in) every 100 years.
This predicted ring may last from 1 million to 100 million years.
Phobos is a small, irregularly shaped object with a mean radius of 11 km (7 mi).

narration.text: Why Phobos circles Mars in under 8 hours.
It orbits just 6,000 kilometres above the surface.
Tides pull it about 2 metres closer every 100 years.
Its mean radius is only 11 kilometres.
Eventually, tidal forces are expected to tear it apart.
The debris could form a ring lasting 1 to 100 million years.
So Mars may swap a moon for a ring.

records.topic: What If the Sahara Turned Green Again?
records.hook: Why the Sahara was green 6,000 years ago.
records.openingLine: Why the Sahara was green 6,000 years ago.
records.secondBeat: A humid period began about 14,500 years ago.
records.scientificMechanism: shifts in Earth's orbit strengthen the African monsoon, bringing rain deep into the Sahara
records.scenarioChange: the African monsoon pushed north again
records.expectedConsequence: grasslands, lakes and wildlife across today's desert
records.coreQuestion: If the Sahara turned green again, what would bring the rain?
records.misconception: The Sahara hasn't always been desert; it was green only a few thousand years ago.
editorialTitles: When the Sahara Was Green
What Turned the Sahara Into Desert

facts.claim: The humid period began about 14,600–14,500 years ago at the end of Heinrich event 1, simultaneously with the Bølling–Allerød warming.
The AHP ended 6,000–5,000 years ago during the Piora Oscillation cold period.
Further discoveries of petroglyphs led desert explorer László Almásy to coin the concept of a Green Sahara in the 1930s.
Some evidence points to an end 5,500 years ago in the Sahel, Arabia, and East Africa.

narration.text: Why the Sahara was green 6,000 years ago.
A humid period began about 14,500 years ago.
Monsoon rains reached far into today's desert.
It ended between 6,000 and 5,000 years ago.
Rock art there shows a greener world.
Shifts in Earth's orbit can move the monsoon again.
So deserts aren't permanent. They follow the rain.

records.topic: What If the Ice Age Came Back?
records.hook: Why Ice Age seas sat 125 metres lower.
records.openingLine: Why Ice Age seas sat 125 metres lower.
records.secondBeat: So much water was locked in ice sheets.
records.scientificMechanism: during glacial maxima, water locked in ice sheets lowers sea level and exposes land bridges
records.scenarioChange: Earth returned to Last Glacial Maximum conditions
records.expectedConsequence: ice over a quarter of the land and seas about 125 metres lower
records.coreQuestion: If the Ice Age came back, what would happen to coastlines?
records.misconception: The last Ice Age wasn't ancient history; its peak was only about 25,000 years ago.
visualScenes: glacier at the Strait of Magellan
editorialTitles: What If the Ice Age Returned
When Seas Were 125 Metres Lower

facts.claim: According to the USGS, permanent summer ice covered around 8% of Earth's surface and 25% of the land area during the last glacial maximum.
The USGS also states that sea level was about 125 meters (410 ft) lower than today (2012).
Glacier fluctuations around the Strait of Magellan suggest the peak in glacial surface area was constrained to between 25,200 and 23,100 years ago.
Decline of the West Antarctica ice sheet occurred between 15,000 and 14,000 years ago, consistent with evidence for another abrupt rise in the sea level around 14,500 years ago.

narration.text: Why Ice Age seas sat 125 metres lower.
So much water was locked in ice sheets.
Ice covered about 25% of the land.
The peak came between 25,200 and 23,100 years ago.
Bring it back, and today's ports would sit far inland.
Land bridges would reappear between continents.
So coastlines are just where the ice happens to leave the sea.

records.topic: What If It Never Rained Again?
records.hook: Why one desert went from 1570 to 1971 dry.
records.openingLine: Why one desert went from 1570 to 1971 dry.
records.scientificMechanism: cold ocean currents and mountain rain shadows block moisture from reaching some deserts
records.scenarioChange: a place went centuries without significant rain
records.expectedConsequence: a landscape so dry it's used to test Mars equipment
records.coreQuestion: If it never rained again, what would the land look like?
records.misconception: The driest place on Earth isn't the Sahara; it's the Atacama.
visualScenes: Mars rover test in the desert
editorialTitles: The Desert That Went 400 Years Without Rain
Why the Atacama Is Driest

facts.claim: Average annual rainfall is around 15 mm (0.6 in) per year, and some weather stations in the desert have never recorded rain.
Evidence suggests the desert may have received no significant rainfall from 1570 to 1971.
It covers an area of 105,000 km2, rising to 128,000 km2 if the barren lower slopes of the Andes are included.
Some locations receive only 1 to 3 mm (0.04 to 0.12 in) in a year.

narration.text: Why one desert went from 1570 to 1971 dry.
That's the Atacama, in Chile.
It averages about 15 millimetres of rain a year.
Some places get only 1 to 3 millimetres.
Some weather stations there have never recorded rain.
Without rain, soil stays almost lifeless.
So the driest place on Earth sits beside an ocean.

records.topic: What If Buildings Grew in the Sun?
records.hook: Why the Eiffel Tower leans 18 centimetres in sunshine.
records.openingLine: Why the Eiffel Tower leans 18 centimetres in sunshine.
records.secondBeat: The Sun heats one side of its iron frame.
records.scientificMechanism: metal expands when heated, so the sunlit side of a steel structure grows longer than the shaded side
records.scenarioChange: a steel tower was heated unevenly by the Sun
records.expectedConsequence: its top leans away from the sunny side by centimetres
records.coreQuestion: If buildings grew in the Sun, how much would a steel tower move?
records.misconception: Big structures aren't rigid; they breathe with temperature.
editorialTitles: Why the Eiffel Tower Moves in the Sun
The Metal Towers That Breathe With Heat

facts.claim: Depending on the ambient temperature, the top of the tower may shift away from the sun by up to 18 cm (7 in) due to thermal expansion of the metal on the side facing the sun.
The tower is 330 metres (1,083 ft) tall, about the same height as an 81-storey building, and the tallest structure in Paris.
Its base is square, measuring 125 metres (410 ft) on each side.
It was the first structure in the world to surpass both the 200-metre and 300-metre mark in height.

narration.text: Why the Eiffel Tower leans 18 centimetres in sunshine.
The Sun heats one side of its iron frame.
That side expands, tilting the top away from the sun.
The tower is 330 metres tall.
Its base spans 125 metres on each side.
Bridges need expansion joints for the same reason.
So even giant structures move with the weather.

records.topic: What If You Melted a Diamond?
records.secondBeat: It also needs about 10 million atmospheres of pressure.
records.scientificMechanism: diamond's strong carbon bonds only give way at extreme pressures and temperatures
records.scenarioChange: a diamond was heated and squeezed to extremes
records.expectedConsequence: at about 1 TPa and 50,000 °C, it becomes a metallic fluid
records.coreQuestion: If you melted a diamond, what would it turn into?
records.misconception: Diamonds aren't forever in every condition; extreme pressure and heat can melt them.
editorialTitles: What It Takes to Melt a Diamond
Why Diamonds Are So Hard to Destroy

facts.claim: Results published in Nature Physics in 2010 suggest that, at ultra-high pressures and temperatures (about 10 million atmospheres or 1 TPa and 50,000 °C), diamond melts into a metallic fluid.
Most natural diamonds have ages between 1 billion and 3.5 billion years.
At 0 K, the transition is predicted to occur at 1100 GPa.
Experiments have found that diamond, in the presence of H2O passes through an intermediate linear carbon phase.

narration.text: Why melting diamond takes 50,000 °C.
It also needs about 10 million atmospheres of pressure.
Diamond's carbon atoms are locked in a rigid lattice.
Under those conditions, it becomes a metallic fluid.
Most natural diamonds are 1 to 3.5 billion years old.
Conditions like that exist deep inside giant planets.
So diamonds may rain and melt in places we can't visit.

records.topic: What If You Never Stopped Growing?
records.hook: Why one man reached 2.72 metres tall.
records.openingLine: Why one man reached 2.72 metres tall.
records.scientificMechanism: excess growth hormone keeps bones lengthening, straining the heart and circulation
records.scenarioChange: a person kept growing throughout life
records.expectedConsequence: record height with serious health strain
records.coreQuestion: If you never stopped growing, how tall could you get?
records.misconception: Extreme height isn't just impressive; it puts heavy strain on the body.
visualScenes: tallest man beside an average man
editorialTitles: The Tallest Man Who Ever Lived
Why You Can't Just Keep Growing

facts.claim: Wadlow's height was 8 ft 11.1 in (2.72 m) while his weight reached 439 lb (199 kg) at his death at age 22.
By the time of his graduation in 1936, he was 8 ft 4 in (254 cm).
On June 27, 1940 (18 days before his death), he was measured by doctors at 8 ft 11.1 in (2.72 m).
Robert Wadlow was the tallest person in recorded history.

narration.text: Why one man reached 2.72 metres tall.
Robert Wadlow never stopped growing.
By 1936, he was already 254 centimetres.
He weighed 199 kilograms.
Excess growth hormone kept his bones lengthening.
In later years, he needed leg braces to walk.
He died at 22, just 18 days after his last measurement.
So the body has a size limit for good reasons.

records.hook: Why only one person is verified past 120.
records.openingLine: Why only one person is verified past 120.
records.secondBeat: Jeanne Calment lived 122 years and 164 days.
records.scientificMechanism: extreme longevity combines genetics, luck and slow ageing
records.expectedConsequence: a life spanning from horse carriages to the internet age
records.coreQuestion: If you lived to 122, what would you have seen?
records.misconception: No one has been verified to live past 122; claims of older ages lack proof.
editorialTitles: The Longest Human Life Ever Verified
What 122 Years Looks Like

facts.claim: Jeanne Louise Calment (21 February 1875 – 4 August 1997) was a French supercentenarian who is the oldest person in recorded history whose age has been verified.
After Calment's death, at 122 years and 164 days, then almost 117-year-old Canadian woman Marie-Louise Meilleur became the oldest validated living person.
Calment is the only person in history who has been verified to have reached the age of 120 years.
Van Gogh's move to Arles occurred from February 1888 to April 1889 when she was 13 and 14 years old.

narration.text: Why only one person is verified past 120.
Jeanne Calment lived 122 years and 164 days.
She was born in 1875 and died in 1997.
As a teenager, she crossed paths with Van Gogh in Arles.
She lived from horse carriages to the space age.
Longevity like hers mixes genes, habits and luck.
So 122 may be close to the human limit.

records.topic: What If We Built a Star on Earth?
records.hook: One gram of fusion fuel: 11 tonnes of coal.
records.openingLine: One gram of fusion fuel: 11 tonnes of coal.
records.secondBeat: That's what ITER, in France, aims to harness.
records.scientificMechanism: a tokamak confines plasma with magnetic fields so hydrogen isotopes can fuse
records.expectedConsequence: proof of large-scale fusion, still short of a working power plant
records.coreQuestion: If we built a star on Earth, what would it cost, and what would it prove?
records.misconception: ITER isn't a power plant; it's an experiment to prove fusion at scale.
editorialTitles: The €20 Billion Machine Building a Star
What ITER Will and Won't Prove

facts.claim: One gram of deuterium-tritium fuel mixture in the process of nuclear fusion produces 90,000-kilowatt hours of energy, or the equivalent of 11 tonnes of coal.
ITER was originally expected to cost approximately €5 billion.
Delays, the rising price of raw materials, and changes to the initial design have seen the official budget estimate rise to between €18 billion and €20 billion.
Construction of the ITER complex in France started in 2013, and assembly of the tokamak began in 2020.

narration.text: One gram of fusion fuel: 11 tonnes of coal.
That's what ITER, in France, aims to harness.
It holds plasma in magnetic fields inside a tokamak.
Construction began in 2013.
The budget grew from €5 billion to €18 to 20 billion.
It's an experiment, not a power station.
So building a star on Earth starts with proving it can burn.

records.topic: What If Sunlight Could Push a Spaceship?
records.hook: Why a 2010 spacecraft flew on sunlight alone.
records.openingLine: Why a 2010 spacecraft flew on sunlight alone.
records.secondBeat: Japan's IKAROS unfurled a huge, thin solar sail.
records.scientificMechanism: photons carry momentum, so a large thin sail feels a tiny but constant push from sunlight
records.scenarioChange: spacecraft sailed on sunlight instead of fuel
records.expectedConsequence: slow but endless acceleration without propellant
records.coreQuestion: If sunlight could push a spaceship, how would you steer it?
records.misconception: Light has no mass, but it still carries momentum that can push a sail.
editorialTitles: The First Spacecraft to Sail on Sunlight
How Light Can Push a Spaceship

facts.claim: The spacecraft was launched on 20 May 2010, aboard an H-IIA rocket, together with the Akatsuki (Venus Climate Orbiter) probe.
IKAROS spun at 20–25 revolutions per minute and finished unfurling its sail on 10 June 2010.
On 9 July 2010, JAXA confirmed that IKAROS was being accelerated by its solar sail, and on 23 July announced successful attitude control.
On 8 December 2010, IKAROS flew by Venus at a distance of 80,800 km (50,200 mi), successfully completing its planned mission.

narration.text: Why a 2010 spacecraft flew on sunlight alone.
Japan's IKAROS unfurled a huge, thin solar sail.
It spun at 20 to 25 turns a minute to spread it.
Light carries momentum, so each photon gives a tiny push.
It passed Venus at 80,800 kilometres that December.
No fuel means it can keep accelerating for years.
So sunlight can be both power and propulsion.

records.topic: What If an Alien Object Flew Past Earth?
records.hook: Why the first interstellar visitor was already leaving.
records.openingLine: Why the first interstellar visitor was already leaving.
records.secondBeat: ʻOumuamua was spotted in 2017, heading away from the Sun.
records.scientificMechanism: an object on a hyperbolic path enters the Solar System from interstellar space and leaves again
records.scenarioChange: an interstellar object passed near Earth
records.expectedConsequence: a brief visit too fast to catch, raising more questions than answers
records.coreQuestion: If an object from another star flew past Earth, could we catch it?
records.misconception: ʻOumuamua wasn't a comet as first thought; it showed no coma.
visualScenes: hyperbolic orbit through the Solar System
editorialTitles: The First Visitor From Another Star
Why We Couldn't Catch ʻOumuamua

facts.claim: 1I/ʻOumuamua is the first confirmed interstellar object detected passing through the Solar System.
When it was first observed, it was about 33 million km from Earth (about 85 times as far away as the Moon) and already heading away from the Sun.
ʻOumuamua is a small object estimated to be between 100 and 1,000 metres long, with its width and thickness both estimated between 35 and 167 metres.
Its speed relative to the Sun when in interstellar space was about 94,800 km/h.
Originally classified as comet C/2017 U1, it was later reclassified as asteroid A/2017 U1 due to the absence of a coma.

narration.text: Why the first interstellar visitor was already leaving.
ʻOumuamua was spotted in 2017, heading away from the Sun.
It was 33 million kilometres away when first seen.
It travels about 94,800 kilometres per hour in interstellar space.
It may be 100 to 1,000 metres long.
It showed no comet tail, so it was reclassified.
So visitors from other stars pass by, and we barely notice.

records.topic: What If Something Was Pulling Our Galaxy?
records.hook: Why galaxies drift toward one hidden region of space.
records.openingLine: Why galaxies drift toward one hidden region of space.
records.secondBeat: Astronomers call it the Great Attractor.
records.scientificMechanism: a large concentration of mass draws galaxies toward it, adding motion on top of cosmic expansion
records.scenarioChange: we mapped what's pulling the Milky Way
records.expectedConsequence: a hidden mass concentration behind our own galaxy's dust
records.coreQuestion: If something was pulling our galaxy, what would it be?
records.misconception: Galaxies don't only drift apart; nearby mass concentrations tug them too.
visualScenes: galaxy flow arrows toward a region
Milky Way dust hiding the view
editorialTitles: The Great Attractor Pulling Our Galaxy
What Lies Behind the Milky Way's Dust

facts.claim: It lies in the general direction of the Norma Cluster and the Hydra–Centaurus Supercluster, approximately 150–250 million light-years from the Milky Way.
Measured values vary with position and can range from approximately +700 km/s to −700 km/s relative to a model of uniform cosmic expansion.
The group studied approximately 400 elliptical galaxies using the Dn–sigma relation.
Infrared surveys identified galaxies whose visible light was obscured by Galactic dust, while radio observations detected the 21-centimeter line emitted by neutral hydrogen.

narration.text: Why galaxies drift toward one hidden region of space.
Astronomers call it the Great Attractor.
It lies about 150 to 250 million light-years away.
Galaxy motions there differ by up to 700 kilometres per second.
Our own galaxy's dust hides it from ordinary telescopes.
Infrared and radio surveys had to peer through.
So even galaxies get tugged by unseen neighbours.

records.topic: What If All the Ants Disappeared?
records.hook: Why there may be 22,000 species of ants.
records.openingLine: Why there may be 22,000 species of ants.
records.secondBeat: Only about 13,800 have been described so far.
records.scientificMechanism: ants aerate soil, spread seeds, recycle dead matter and control other insects
records.expectedConsequence: slower soil turnover, fewer dispersed seeds and more pests
records.coreQuestion: If all the ants disappeared, what would stop working?
records.misconception: Ants aren't just pests; ecosystems rely on them.
editorialTitles: What If Ants Vanished
The Tiny Engineers Running the Soil

facts.claim: More than 13,800 of an estimated total of 22,000 species have been described.
Ants diversified extensively during the Angiosperm Terrestrial Revolution and assumed ecological dominance around 60 million years ago.
By the Oligocene and Miocene, ants had come to represent 20–40% of all insects found in major fossil deposits.
The specimen, trapped in amber dating back to around 92 million years ago, has features found in some wasps, but not found in modern ants.

narration.text: Why there may be 22,000 species of ants.
Only about 13,800 have been described so far.
Ants became ecologically dominant around 60 million years ago.
They later made up 20 to 40% of fossil insects.
They churn soil and carry seeds into the ground.
Without them, dead matter and pests would pile up.
So some of Earth's key engineers are only millimetres long.
